title: Conversions, Booleans and Input
subtitle: Five guided reading lessons, a ten-question quiz, and a ten-task practical assessment.

sections.title: Boolean values and meaningful names
sections.intro: Objective: store a yes/no fact and inspect its type.
paragraphs: A bool represents one of two values: True or False. Capital letters matter. Use these values for facts such as whether a ticket is paid.
Choose a name that explains the fact: is_ready is clearer than x. Python names are case-sensitive, cannot contain spaces, and cannot start with a digit.
Use int for whole counts, float for measurements, str for text and bool for yes/no facts. A value’s type determines which operations make sense.

print(is_ready)
print(type(is_ready))

sections.title: Convert text into useful numbers
sections.intro: Objective: convert text with int(), float() and str().
paragraphs: Text from a form looks like digits but cannot be added to a number directly. int("12") creates the integer 12; float("12.5") creates a decimal value.
Conversion creates a new value. The original text remains text unless you assign the converted result back to the same name.
int("12.5") raises ValueError because a decimal string is not an integer spelling. int(12.9) instead truncates a numeric float toward zero; it does not round.

sections.title: Read prepared input safely
sections.intro: Objective: use input() and understand its string result.
paragraphs: In terminal Python, input() waits for one line typed by the user. It returns text even when that line contains digits.
In this browser, enter lines in Prepared input before running. Each input() consumes one line. The worker never opens a blocking dialog; running out of lines raises a clear error.
Use fictional practice values. The input stays in this browser worker and is not sent to FastAPI. Convert numeric text before arithmetic; malformed input can still raise ValueError.

sections.title: Follow values through an update
sections.intro: Objective: trace assignments without losing the original meaning.
paragraphs: Assignment evaluates the right side first, then binds the name on the left. After balance = balance + 5, future lookups see the new balance.
Keep units in names: price_dollars and quantity explain a calculation better than a and b. A receipt total is numeric data; a label is text.
When debugging, inspect type(value) as well as print(value). The displays of 12 and "12" look alike but their types differ.

title: Python Operators
subtitle: Five guided reading lessons, a ten-question quiz, and a ten-task practical assessment.

sections.title: Arithmetic for everyday quantities
sections.intro: Objective: combine numeric values using +, -, *, / and //.
paragraphs: An operator asks Python to perform an operation on values called operands. Addition combines quantities; subtraction finds a difference; multiplication scales a quantity.
True division / returns a float even when the division is exact. Floor division // rounds a quotient down, so -7 // 2 is -4 rather than -3.
For a shopping basket, multiply unit price by quantity before combining subtotals. Use small known examples to check a formula before trusting a large result.

print(price * quantity)

print(7 // 2)

sections.title: Remainders, powers and precedence
sections.intro: Objective: group calculations deliberately and use % and **.
paragraphs: Modulus % gives the remainder associated with floor division. For positive counts, count % size tells you how many items remain after filling groups.
Exponentiation ** raises a base to a power: 2 ** 3 is eight. It is not multiplication by three. Powers happen before multiplication, which happens before addition.
Parentheses override the default order. Read 2 + 3 * 4 as 2 + (3 * 4); write (2 + 3) * 4 when the addition must happen first.

sections.mistakes: ^ is a bitwise operation in Python, not the power operator. Use ** for powers.
sections.practice: Calculate a square with ** and check how parentheses change a sum.

sections.title: Compare values to get a Boolean
sections.intro: Objective: ask questions using ==, !=, <, <=, > and >=.
paragraphs: A comparison produces True or False. Use == to ask whether two values are equal, and != to ask whether they differ.
The equals sign = assigns a value. It cannot replace == in an ordinary comparison expression. Inclusive comparisons <= and >= include the boundary itself.
Comparisons can be chained: 0 <= temperature <= 30 means both bounds hold. Prefer testing the exact boundary as well as a value on either side.

print(age >= 18)

print(age != 21)

sections.title: Combine facts with logic and update values
sections.intro: Objective: combine Booleans with and, or, not; update using +=.
paragraphs: and requires both conditions to be true. or accepts either condition. not reverses a truth value. Parentheses make grouped rules easier to read.
For a library loan, membership and an available copy might both be required. A staff override could use or, but write the policy in words before coding it.
Augmented assignment updates an existing value: score += 2 behaves like score = score + 2 for an integer. The name must already exist.

sections.intro: Objective: combine operators into a tested real-world calculation.
paragraphs: When several people share a bill, divide the total by the number of people. Confirm the divisor is not zero before using it in a real application.
Use parentheses to show which subtotal a surcharge applies to. Check units: a fraction such as 0.1 is a ten-percent rate, while 10 is ten whole units.

Final assessment: the quiz checks operator meaning and boundaries. The final lab task combines integer grouping, remainder and a labeled result. Test changed inputs to catch a formula that only works once.

title: Strings
subtitle: Five guided reading lessons, a ten-question quiz, and a ten-task practical assessment.

sections.title: Create and join text
sections.intro: Objective: distinguish text literals from variables and concatenate strings.
paragraphs: A string is a sequence of Unicode characters. Single and double quotes both delimit a string; the delimiters are not part of the stored value.
The + operator joins strings without inserting spaces. Include the separating space yourself or pass separate arguments to print, which inserts a space by default.
Strings are immutable. An operation returns a new string; it does not edit the original string in place. Assign the result when you want to keep it.

last = "Lovelace"
full = first + " " + last
print(full)

sections.title: Index and slice a sequence
sections.intro: Objective: select characters using zero-based positions and slices.
paragraphs: The first character is at index zero. A negative index counts from the end, so word[-1] selects the last character.
A slice word[start:stop] includes start and excludes stop. Omitting start begins at zero; omitting stop continues to the end. Slices that extend past an edge are safely shortened.
A single index outside the string raises IndexError. Before indexing real input, consider whether it might be empty. len(word) gives the character count.

print(word[0])
print(word[-1])
print(word[1:4])

sections.title: Format values with f-strings
sections.intro: Objective: embed values and calculations inside readable text.
paragraphs: Put f before a quoted string to allow expressions inside braces. Python evaluates each expression and inserts a text representation of its result.
An f-string can mix text and numbers without manually calling str for each one. Ordinary strings without the f prefix display the braces literally.
A format specifier controls presentation: {price:.2f} displays two decimal places. Formatting changes the text representation, not the stored numeric value.

sections.title: Clean text with methods
sections.intro: Objective: use strip(), lower(), upper() and replace() to normalize text.
paragraphs: A method is a function accessed through a value using a dot. raw.strip() returns text without leading or trailing whitespace.
lower() and upper() return versions with changed case. They are useful when comparing user entries, but keep original text if its original capitalization matters.
replace(old, new) substitutes matching pieces. Chaining methods uses the result of each previous method. None of these calls changes the original string unless you reassign it.

print(clean)
print(clean.replace("python", "coding"))

sections.title: Practical application: format a message
sections.intro: Objective: combine escaped characters, cleanup and formatting.
paragraphs: An escape sequence begins with a backslash inside a string. \n represents a newline, \t a tab and \\ a literal backslash. These are characters in the string, not separate Python statements.
Choose the outer quote style to reduce escapes: a double-quoted string can contain an apostrophe directly. A backslash can also escape a matching quote.
Final assessment: the quiz checks indexing, formatting and method behavior. The final lab task builds a cleaned contact label and a formatted numeric total from changing data.

title: Conditional Statements
subtitle: Five guided reading lessons, a ten-question quiz, and a ten-task practical assessment.

sections.title: Choose a path with if
sections.intro: Objective: run a block only when a condition is true.
paragraphs: An if statement evaluates a condition. When the result is true, Python runs the indented block beneath it. When false, Python skips that block.
The header ends with a colon. Indentation groups the statements in the block; use four spaces consistently. A line back at the outer indentation is outside the block.
Test both a true and a false condition. A program that works once may still contain an off-by-one boundary error.
sections.code:
age = 18
if age >= 18:
    print("Adult")

sections.title: Give an alternative with else
sections.intro: Objective: select exactly one of two branches.
paragraphs: else supplies the alternative when the if condition is false. It has a colon but no condition, because it covers all remaining cases.
Align else with its if, then indent the body. Exactly one of the two blocks runs for each evaluation.
A common decision is whether a balance covers a cost. Equality belongs in the affordable branch when a balance exactly equal to the cost is enough.

sections.title: Order several cases with elif
sections.intro: Objective: make an ordered multiway decision.
paragraphs: elif means else if. Python checks conditions from top to bottom and executes only the first matching branch in an if/elif/else chain.
Order thresholds from the most restrictive to the least restrictive. If score >= 50 comes before score >= 80, a score of ninety matches fifty first.
The final else is a fallback. Think about every possible input, including the exact boundaries, before deciding what the fallback should mean.

sections.title: Combine and nest decisions
sections.intro: Objective: express compound rules and nested checks clearly.
paragraphs: Use and when two facts must hold, or when either fact is sufficient, and not to reverse a fact. Parentheses make mixed rules readable.
A nested if is evaluated only inside a selected outer branch. For a delivery, first check that the address is supported; only then inspect an express-service option.
Prefer one combined condition for a simple two-fact rule. Nest when each stage needs its own explanation or different feedback.

sections.title: Practical application: admission policy
sections.intro: Objective: translate a written policy into complete decisions.
paragraphs: Write the rule in plain language first: a ticket is required; children below twelve use the child rate; everyone else uses the standard rate.
Check admission before computing the rate. Test a missing ticket, the age just below the threshold and the exact threshold itself.

Final assessment: the quiz checks branch selection and indentation. The final lab task combines ticket and age decisions and must respond correctly to changed data. Failed submissions can be retried without losing earlier passes.

exercises.title: Age decision
exercises.description: Assign age = 18. Print Adult if age >= 18, otherwise print Minor.
hints: Compare age to the inclusive bound.
exercises.explanation: The exact adulthood boundary is included.

exercises.title: Even or odd
exercises.description: Assign number = 8. Print Even if divisible by two, otherwise Odd.
hints: A remainder of zero means divisibility.
exercises.explanation: Remainder classifies both positive and negative integers by parity.

exercises.title: Enough funds
exercises.description: Assign balance = 10 and cost = 10. Print Affordable when balance covers cost, otherwise Save more.
hints: Display exactly one of the labels.
exercises.explanation: Equality is an affordable purchase.

exercises.title: Three score bands
exercises.description: Assign score = 80. Print Excellent for scores >= 80, Pass for scores >= 50, otherwise Retry.
hints: Use elif for the middle band.
exercises.explanation: Ordered branches prevent a high score being captured by a lower threshold.

exercises.title: Sign of a number
exercises.description: Assign number = 0. Print Positive, Negative or Zero according to its sign.
hints: The remaining case is exactly zero.
exercises.explanation: A complete chain handles zero explicitly.

exercises.title: Two requirements
exercises.description: Assign age = 20 and has_ticket = True. Print Enter only when age >= 18 and a ticket is present; otherwise print Wait.
hints: Use an alternative for failed requirements.
exercises.explanation: A ticket alone or an age alone is insufficient.

exercises.title: Either qualification
exercises.description: Assign is_member = False and has_coupon = True. Print Discount if either fact is true, otherwise Full price.
hints: Reject only when neither fact holds.
exercises.explanation: or accepts either qualification.

exercises.title: Choose delivery
exercises.description: Assign supported = True and express = False. Print Unavailable if not supported; otherwise Express if express is true, or Standard if false.
hints: Check support before the express option.
Align each else with its matching if.
A supported nonexpress request uses Standard.
exercises.explanation: The outer rule prevents express requests bypassing address support.

exercises.title: Comfortable temperature
exercises.description: Assign temperature = 20. Print Comfortable when 18 <= temperature <= 25, otherwise Adjust.
hints: Use a chained comparison or and.
exercises.explanation: The range has two inclusive boundaries.

exercises.title: Assessment: admission policy
exercises.description: Assign age = 12 and has_ticket = True. Without a ticket print Ticket required. With a ticket, print Child rate below age 12, otherwise Standard rate.
hints: Check the ticket before the rate.
